questions.q: A driver was involved in an accident in which a pedestrian was injured. What is their immediate duty?
options: Stop only if the pedestrian asks them to
Keep driving and notify the police within 24 hours
Stop immediately, give help, call the emergency services and notify the police as soon as possible
Stop only if they think they are at fault for the accident
questions.explain: Regulation 144 requires you to stop immediately, help, call the emergency services and notify the police as soon as possible — regardless of who is at fault.

questions.q: An accident damaged a parked vehicle whose owner was not present, with no bodily injury. What must the driver do?
options: Notify the police within a week
There is no duty to report at all, since there are no casualties
Leave a written note and notify the nearest police station within {{fact:accident.property_damage.report_hours}}
Leave a note without notifying the police
questions.explain: When the owner of the damaged property was not present, you must leave a written note and notify the nearest police station within {{fact:accident.property_damage.report_hours}} (reg. 145).

questions.q: A driver involved in an accident with bodily injury did not show their insurance certificate at the scene. By when must they report this to the police and show it?
options: {{fact:accident.insurance_certificate.report_hours}}
There is no time limit, it can be done at any stage
Only if the police ask for it
One week
questions.explain: Under the Motor Vehicle Insurance Ordinance, section 40, you must report the accident and show the insurance certificate within {{fact:accident.insurance_certificate.report_hours}}.

questions.q: A driver did not show their insurance certificate within {{fact:accident.insurance_certificate.report_hours}}. How many more days do they still have to show it themselves at the station, to avoid conviction for not showing it?
options: A further {{fact:accident.insurance_certificate.late_presentation_days}}
No further option
A further month
One further day
questions.explain: The Motor Vehicle Insurance Ordinance, section 40, allows a further {{fact:accident.insurance_certificate.late_presentation_days}} to show it in person at the station where the report was filed.

questions.q: A driver is injured in an accident and unable to act. From what age must a passenger in the vehicle call and summon the emergency services themselves?
options: The duty applies to every passenger, at any age
From age 12
From age 21
From age {{fact:accident.passenger_duty.min_age|n}}
questions.explain: Traffic Ordinance, section 64A1, places the duty on a passenger aged {{fact:accident.passenger_duty.min_age|n}} or older, and only if the driver themselves did not stop and call for help.

questions.q: A driver is involved in an accident with a casualty, but is sure the accident is not their fault. What is correct?
options: They must stop and act according to the law in any case — the question of fault is examined later
It is enough to call the police without stopping
The duty to stop applies only to the driver at fault
They may leave the scene, since they are not at fault
questions.explain: The duty to stop, help and notify the police (reg. 144) exists regardless of the question of fault. Leaving the scene of an accident with a casualty is a serious offence even for someone who is not at fault.

questions.q: Where should you place a warning triangle beside a vehicle that has stopped after an accident?
options: There is no duty to place a triangle in an accident, only in a mechanical breakdown
Right next to the vehicle only
Only if it is raining
Where it will be seen from at least {{fact:equip.triangle.visibility}} by approaching vehicles
questions.explain: Regulation 70 requires the triangle to be placed where it will be seen from at least {{fact:equip.triangle.visibility}}.

questions.q: When must you wear a high-visibility vest after an accident?
options: When getting out of the vehicle on a non-urban road
Always, even inside the vehicle
Only at night
Only if there are casualties
questions.explain: Traffic Ordinance, section 65B, requires a high-visibility vest when getting out of the vehicle on a non-urban road — day and night alike.

questions.q: Where is it correct to stand after marking the vehicle with hazard lights and a triangle?
options: Between the two vehicles involved
In the traffic lane, to stop approaching vehicles
Beside the vehicle, to keep watch over it
Off the road, behind a safety barrier if there is one
questions.explain: Stand off the road, behind a barrier if there is one, and face the oncoming traffic — not in the lane and not between the vehicles.

questions.q: A road accident has a casualty and also a strong smell of fuel. Who do you call?
options: The police {{fact:emergency.police}}, Magen David Adom {{fact:emergency.mda}} and Fire and Rescue Services {{fact:emergency.fire_and_rescue}}
Only the police, {{fact:emergency.police}}
Only the insurance company
Only Magen David Adom, {{fact:emergency.mda}}
questions.explain: A road accident is always reported to the police; casualties also require Magen David Adom; and a fire hazard or fuel leak also requires Fire and Rescue Services.

questions.q: How many people should ideally talk to the emergency dispatcher when several passers-by have stopped to help at an accident?
options: One person, to avoid confusion
Only the driver involved, even if they are injured
No one — it is better to wait for someone else to call
Everyone together, so the dispatcher gets as much information as possible
questions.explain: When several people have stopped to help, it is best for one person to pass the information to the dispatcher in an orderly way — this saves time and prevents confusion.

questions.q: You arrive at the scene of an accident with a casualty. What is the correct first step?
options: Remove their helmet or clothing to check for injuries
Rush over immediately and move the injured person to somewhere more comfortable
Check that there is no further hazard (traffic, fire, fuel) before approaching
Give them water to drink so they feel better
questions.explain: Before approaching an injured person, check for further hazards. Approaching carelessly can turn the helper into another casualty.

questions.q: When is it permitted to move an injured person at the scene of an accident?
options: Only if there is immediate danger, such as fire or a vehicle that might move
It is never permitted to move an injured person, even if there is fire
Only if they ask you to
Always, so they feel more comfortable
questions.explain: Do not move an injured person except in immediate danger. Unnecessary movement can make an injury worse, especially to the spine.

questions.q: A motorcyclist is injured and still wearing their helmet. What is correct to do?
options: Remove the helmet immediately to check the head
Break the helmet to get it off easily
Leave the helmet in place and do not touch it, unless it is blocking their breathing
Remove the helmet only if they are conscious
questions.explain: Removing a helmet from someone who is injured can make a neck or spinal injury worse. Leave it in place, unless it is blocking their breathing, and wait for a professional crew.

questions.q: In which of the following vehicles does the law require first aid equipment?
options: Every motor vehicle, with no exceptions
A private car
A motorcycle
A public bus
questions.explain: Regulation 369A requires first aid equipment in a taxi, a touring vehicle, a desert vehicle, a tour bus, a security vehicle and a public bus — not in a private car.

questions.q: You smell smoke and see it coming from under the bonnet while driving. What do you do first?
options: Open the bonnet immediately to check the source
Keep driving fast to reach the nearest garage
Get off the road, switch off the engine, and get all the passengers out and away
Open the windows and air out the vehicle while still driving
questions.explain: If you suspect a fire, get off the road, switch off the engine and move away immediately. Do not open a bonnet with smoke coming out of it — this can make the fire flare up.

questions.q: Is a fire extinguisher compulsory in a private car?
options: Yes, in every private car
No — a fire extinguisher is compulsory in a taxi, a commercial vehicle and a bus, not in a private car
Only in a new private car from the last two years
Only if the car has air conditioning
questions.explain: Regulation 370 exempts a private car, a motorcycle and a tractor from the fire-extinguisher requirement, while a taxi, a commercial vehicle and a bus must carry one.

questions.q: A vehicle drives into a deep pool of water and starts to sink. What is important to do immediately?
options: Force the door open immediately, even with a large pressure difference
Open or break a window immediately, before the electrics fail and the water rises
Try to start the engine and drive out of the water
Wait for the vehicle to sink fully and only then open a door
questions.explain: Power windows stop working once water reaches the electrical system, so open or break a window immediately. A door is hard to open while there is still a large pressure difference.

questions.q: A vehicle sinking in water has a child and an adult inside. Who gets out first?
options: Wait for a rescue crew before anyone gets out
The adult, so they can help from outside
It does not matter who goes first, as long as everyone gets out together
The child, and anyone who finds it hard to move on their own
questions.explain: Children and passengers who find it hard to move on their own get out first, because the time before the vehicle fully sinks is limited.

questions.q: What is most important when you notice a vehicle fire, before trying to put it out?
options: Photograph the fire for the insurance claim
Open all the windows so the smoke can get out
Move the vehicle to the verge before getting out of it
Get all the passengers out and move away to a safe distance
questions.explain: Before any attempt to put out a fire, get all the passengers out and move away to a safe distance. Fire can spread within seconds.

questions.q: What is the main difference between compulsory insurance and comprehensive insurance?
options: Comprehensive insurance is compulsory for every vehicle; compulsory insurance is voluntary
Compulsory insurance covers only damage to property, not to the body
There is no difference, both names describe the same insurance
Compulsory insurance covers bodily injury only and is required for every vehicle; comprehensive insurance is voluntary and also covers the vehicle itself
questions.explain: Compulsory insurance, required by law, covers bodily injury only. Comprehensive insurance is a voluntary addition that also covers damage to the vehicle itself, and sometimes theft and weather damage.

questions.q: What is correct regarding driving without valid compulsory insurance?
options: It is allowed for a short trip only, such as a trip to the garage
It is a serious offence, even if no accident happened
It is allowed if you have comprehensive insurance
It is allowed, as long as no accident actually happens
questions.explain: Driving without valid compulsory insurance is a serious offence in itself, regardless of whether an accident happened.

questions.q: When is it best to photograph the scene of the accident and the damage?
options: Before the vehicles move from their position, if it is possible and safe
Only after the police arrive
There is no need to photograph, a verbal description to the insurer is enough
Only if it is clear who is at fault
questions.explain: Documenting early, before the vehicles move, preserves the exact state of the scene and prevents later disputes.

questions.q: Why is it worth collecting witnesses' details at an accident, even if there is no camera that recorded it?
options: Because the testimony of an uninvolved person can settle a dispute about fault
It is only needed if there are casualties
So they sign to confirm the driver is not at fault
Witnesses have no value, only the police can determine fault
questions.explain: The testimony of someone who was not involved in the accident can be important evidence when there is a dispute between the parties about what happened.

questions.q: When is it best to report an accident to the insurance company?
options: Only if the damage is above a certain amount
There is no need to report if you only have compulsory insurance
Only after it is finally clear who is at fault
As soon as possible, even if it is still unclear who is at fault
questions.explain: Report to the insurance company as soon as possible — some policies set a maximum time for reporting, and a delay can harm your cover.
